Encrypt.One is built so that only the recipient can read a secret — not even us. Here is what data passes through the service and what happens to it.

The application server logs only API requests: the request type, the result and the processing time. IP addresses, secret ids, tokens, page addresses and request contents are never logged.

To protect the service from brute force and abuse, the server limits the request rate per IP address. The address is used only in memory and is not stored.

A web server in front of the application may keep a standard access log: IP address, time and page address without the part after #. Such logs are used only to protect against attacks and are kept for a limited time.
Encrypt.One privacy policy: what data the service receives, how long it keeps it and why it can't read your secrets.

The password itself never leaves your browser. From the password and the link key the browser derives two independent values: the encryption key and a check hash (PBKDF2 with 600,000 iterations, then HKDF). Only the hash is sent to the server. The server uses it to check the password but can learn neither the password nor the key.

After three wrong attempts the secret is deleted. The attempt counter is kept in the server memory and belongs to the secret, not to a visitor.

We do not know who created or opened a secret: the service links data to no people, accounts or IP addresses. That is why we cannot find, hand over or delete the data of a particular person. To delete your secret before it expires, open the link page and press “Destroy now”.

Text and an attached file are encrypted in your browser with AES-256-GCM through the built-in Web Crypto API before they are sent. The file name and type are encrypted together with the content.

The server stores only:

  • the encrypted data;
  • the expiry time;
  • whether a file is attached;
  • a password check hash, if you set an opening password.

The decryption key is the part of the link after the # sign. Browsers never send that part to the server, so neither we nor anyone who gains access to the server can decrypt the data. For the same reason we cannot recover a secret if the link is lost.

You send the link yourself, in any way you like. A messenger, email or SMS can be intercepted, and then whoever opens the link first gets the secret. For important data, set an opening password and share it through a different channel.

• Your secret is encrypted in your browser. The server receives only encrypted data and cannot read it.
  • The decryption key lives in the link after the # sign and is never sent to the server.
  • No sign-up, ads, analytics or third-party scripts.
  • A secret is deleted as soon as it is opened or when the chosen period ends.
  • The application server does not log IP addresses or secret ids.
The source code is open on GitHub: you can check how the encryption works or run your own copy.

We use no advertising or analytics cookies. The site stores in your browser only what it needs to work:

  • the lang cookie — your language, if you picked one in the switcher;
  • in localStorage — the color theme, a note that you closed the language banner and notes about links destroyed from this browser;
  • in sessionStorage — a password from the generator while it is carried over to the form on the home page. It is removed right after it is inserted.

Of these, only the language cookie reaches the server, which uses it to pick the page version. You can delete all of it in your browser settings.

The site loads no third-party scripts, fonts, counters or ads: everything, fonts included, is served from our own server. We do not sell or share data with third parties.

The buttons for sending via Telegram, WhatsApp and email, as well as links to sponsor sites, are plain links. An external service gets data only when you click one, and its own policy applies from then on.
